ex-206-1.title: Work done on a toy
ex-206-1.question:
A girl pulls a toy for 0.1 m with a horizontal force of 2 N (Fig a). A boy then pulls the toy for another 0.1 m with a force of 2 N, but his force makes an angle of 30° to the horizontal (Fig b).

(a) Find the work done by the girl and the boy on the toy.

(b) The boy releases the toy and it moves 5 cm forwards before it stops. What is the work done by the boy on the toy in this part of journey?
ex-206-1.answer:
(a) Apply W = Fs cos θ.

Work done by the girl = 2 × 0.1 × cos 0°

= 0.2 J

Work done by the boy = 2 × 0.1 × cos 30°

= 0.173 J

(b) 0
ex-206-1.tips:
Tip

The force acting on the toy by the boy is zero in this part of journey.

ex-206-2.title: Change in energy of an object
ex-206-2.question:
A force F of 10 N acts on an object over a displacement of 2 m towards the left on a rough horizontal surface as shown. The friction f acting on the object is 4 N. What is

the change in energy of the object?
ex-206-2.answer:
Net force along displacement = 10 + (−4) = 6 N (towards the left)

Work done by net force = Fs = 6 × 2 = 12 J

∴ The object gains 12 J of energy.

ex-206-3.title: KE of different objects
ex-206-3.question:
Find the KE of

(a) a 5-kg bowling ball moving at 7 m s−1,

(b) a 4-g bullet moving at 1080 km h−1,

(c) a hydrogen molecule of mass 3.35 × 10−27 kg moving at 1930 m s−1.
ex-206-3.answer:
Apply KE = 12mv2.

(a) KE = 12 × 5 × 72 = 123 J

(b) KE =12×(4×10−3)×(10803.6)2=180 J

(c) KE = 12 × (3.35 × 10–27) × 19302 = 6.24 × 10−21 J
ex-206-3.think: Is the KE of a fast object always larger than that of a slow object? Why?
ex-206-3.thinkAnswer: No. KE=12mv2 depends on mass as well as speed. A fast object of sufficiently small mass can have less KE than a slower, heavier object. For example, the hydrogen molecule in (c) is faster than the bowling ball in (a), but has far less KE.

ex-206-4.title: PE of a hiker
ex-206-4.question:
Johnny of mass 70 kg climbs up a slope. He walks 40 m from point A to point B. A and B are respectively 10 m and 30 m above the ground. Take the gravitational PE at the ground level as zero.

(a) Find Johnny’s gravitational PE at A.

(b) What is the change in gravitational PE of Johnny when he walks from A to B?

(c) Now, take the gravitational PE at B as zero. How are the answers to (a) and (b) affected?
ex-206-4.answer:
(a) Gravitational PE at A = mghA = 70 × 9.81 × 10 = 6870 J

(b) Change in gravitational PE = mgΔh = 70 × 9.81 × (30 − 10) = 13 700 J

(c) By taking the gravitational PE at B as zero, hA = −20 m

Gravitational PE at A = mghA = 70 × 9.81 × (−20) = −13 700 J

∴ The answer to (a) becomes −13 700 J.

Since Δh is still 20 m, the answer to (b) remains unchanged.

ex-206-5.title: Speed of a pendulum bob
ex-206-5.question:
A pendulum bob is pulled to one side and held at A, which is 20 cm higher than its lowest position B. It is then released.

(a) Find its speed at B.

(b) Find its speed at C on the other side which is 10 cm above B.
ex-206-5.answer:
Method 1

Take the PE at B as zero.

(a) Consider the motion from A to B.

KE A + PEA = KEB + PEB

0+mghA=12mvB2+0

9.81×0.2=12× vB2

vB=1.98 m s−1

Its speed at B is 1.98 m s-1.

(b) Consider the motion from A to C.

KE A + PEA = KEC + PEC

0+mghA=12mvC2+mghC

9.81×0.2=12× vC2+9.81×0.1

vC=1.40 m s−1

Its speed at C is 1.40 m s-1.

Method 2

(a) Consider the motion from A to B.

Loss in PE = gain in KE

mgΔh=12× m×(v2−u2)

9.81×0.2=12×(v2−02)

v=1.98 m s−1

Its speed at B is 1.98 m s-1.

(b) Consider the motion from A to C.

Loss in PE = gain in KE

mgΔh=12× m×(v2−02)

9.81×(0.2−0.1)=12× v2

v=1.40 m s−1

Its speed at C is 1.40 m s-1.
ex-206-5.tips:
Skill Problem-solving — Method 1

Solving problems with KE 1 + PE1 = KE2 + PE2

① Choose a reference level where PE = 0.

② Determine the speeds and heights of the object at the initial and final positions.

③ Set an equation with KE 1 + PE1 = KE2 + PE2.

④ Solve the equation.

Skill Problem-solving — Method 2

Solving problems with loss in KE / PE = gain in PE / KE

① Determine the speeds of the object at the initial and final positions and its change in height.

② Determine whether the KE and PE of the object has a gain or a loss.

③ Set an equation with loss in KE / PE = gain in PE / KE.

④ Solve the equation.
ex-206-5.think:
1 Can Newton’s second law be applied to solve this problem? Why?

2 Is the following calculation for (a) correct? v2=u2+2as, v2=02+2×9.81×0.2, v=1.98 m s−1.
ex-206-5.thinkAnswer:
1 Newton’s second law applies, but the bob’s acceleration is not constant: both the tension and the direction of motion change. A direct constant-acceleration calculation is therefore unsuitable. Resolving tangentially and integrating m vdvds=mgsinθ along the descending arc gives 12mv2=mgΔ h, reproducing the energy result.

2 No. The numerical answer happens to be correct, but the bob does not fall freely with acceleration g, and 0.2 m is the vertical drop rather than the distance along its curved path. The valid justification is conservation of energy: v=2gΔ h=2×9.81×0.2=1.98 m s−1.

ex-206-6.title: Bungee jumping
ex-206-6.question:
Edwin goes bungee jumping. He is tied to a fixed point C with a light elastic string and then jumps down from C from rest. The elastic string is 40 m long before stretching. The mass of Edwin is 70 kg. Assume that the total mechanical energy of Edwin and the elastic string remains constant.

Edwin passes points X and Y during his fall.

(a) X is 40 m below C. Find Edwin’s speed vX at X.

(b) Y is 117 m below C and Edwin’s speed is 9.95 m s−1 at Y. Find the energy EPEY stored in the elastic string when Edwin is at Y.
ex-206-6.answer:
Take the gravitational PE at Y as zero.

(a) Consider the motion from C to X.

KEC + EPEC + GPEC = KEX + EPEX + GPEX

0 + 0 + mghC = 12mvX2 + 0 + mghX

9.81 × 117 = 12 × vX2 + 9.81 × (117 − 40)

vX = 28.0 m s−1

(b) Consider the motion from C to Y.

KEC + EPEC + GPEC = KEY + EPEY + GPEY

0 + 0 + mghC = 12mvY2 + EPEY + 0

70 × 9.81 × 117 = 12 × 70 × 9.952 + EPEY

EPEY = 76 900 J
ex-206-6.tips:
Tip

EPE = 0 as the string is not

taut yet.
ex-206-6.think:
1 How will the answers change if the GPE at C is taken as zero?

2 Can Newton’s second law of motion be applied to solve (a)? Why?
ex-206-6.thinkAnswer:
1 Neither answer changes. Only differences in GPE affect the motion. With C as zero, GPEX=−mg(40) and GPEY=−mg(117). Energy conservation gives vX=28.0 m s−1 and EPEY=mg(117)−12m(9.95)2=7.69×104 J.

2 Yes. Until Edwin reaches X, the string has not stretched, so its tension is zero. Neglecting air resistance, mg=ma gives a=g. Thus vX2=0+2g(40) and vX=28.0 m s−1.

ex-206-7.title: Energy conversion in car braking
ex-206-7.question:
A car travels on a horizontal road at a speed of 18 m s−1. After the driver applies the brake, the car is brought to a stop in 12 m (stopping distance). Take the mass of the car to be 900 kg. Assume that the friction acting on the car during braking is constant.

(a) Estimate the friction acting on the car.

(b) If the road is wet, the friction acting on the car will be smaller. How will the stopping distance change? Explain briefly.
ex-206-7.answer:
(a) Loss in KE = W against friction f

12m(u2 – v2) = fs

12 × 900 × (182 – 0) = f × 12

f = 12 200 N

The friction acting on the car is 12 200 N.

(b) The work done against friction W needed to stop the car will remain unchanged (equal to initial KE of the car).

By W = fs, the stopping distance s will increase if friction f decreases.
ex-206-7.think: Can Newton’s second law of motion be applied to solve this problem? Why?
ex-206-7.thinkAnswer:
Yes. The friction is constant, so the net force and acceleration are constant. Taking forwards as positive, a=v2−u22s=0−1822×12=−13.5 m s−2. Hence f=m|a|=900×13.5=1.22×104 N, opposite to the motion.

On a wet road the smaller friction produces a smaller deceleration. Since s=mu22f for the same initial speed, the stopping distance increases.

ex-206-8.title: Work done by tension and elastic energy
ex-206-8.question:
Edwin goes bungee jumping again. He is tied to point C with a light elastic string. He jumps down from C from rest, passes point X and then point Y (Fig a). When Edwin is at X, his speed is 28.0 m s−1 and the elastic string starts to stretch. Edwin’s speed reaches 9.95 m s−1 at Y, which is 77 m below X. The mass of Edwin is 70 kg.

Find the average tension T acting on Edwin by the string during his fall from X to Y.
ex-206-8.answer:
Take the gravitational PE at Y as zero.

Consider the total mechanical energy of Edwin.

KEX + PEX = KEY + PEY + W against tension T

12mvX2 + mghX = 12mvY2 + 0 + Ts

12 × 70 × 28.02 + 70 × 9.81 × 77 = 12 × 70 × 9.952 + T × 77

T = 998 N

The average tension T acting on Edwin by the string is 998 N.
ex-206-8.tips:
Tip

As only the mechanical energy of Edwin is considered, the elastic PE of the string is not included in the equation.

ex-206-9.title: Average power
ex-206-9.question:
A woman does 5000 J of work in jogging for 10 s.

(a) Find her average power.

(b) A man also does 5000 J of work in walking for 40 s. Is his power larger or smaller than the woman’s power? Explain without calculation.
ex-206-9.answer:
(a) P = Wt = 500010 = 500 W

(b) The man takes more time t to do the same work W. According to P = Wt,

his power P is smaller.

ex-206-10.title: Power of a car
ex-206-10.question: A car is travelling at a constant velocity of 30 m s−1 on a level road. What is the power output of the car engine if the total resistive force acting on the car is 800 N?
ex-206-10.answer:
Forward force due to the engine = total resistive force = 800 N

Power output = Fv = 800 × 30 = 24 000 W
ex-206-10.tips:
Tip

Since the car is travelling at a constant velocity, the net force is zero.
ex-206-10.think: Tom claims that if the car is travelling at a higher velocity, a smaller force is needed to keep the velocity constant according to P = Fv. Is he correct?
ex-206-10.thinkAnswer: No. At any constant velocity, the driving force must balance the resistive force. The argument F=Pv would require the power P to stay fixed, which is not given. If resistance remains 800 N, the driving force remains 800 N and a higher speed requires greater power. If air resistance increases with speed, a larger driving force is needed.

ex-206-11.title: Power and conservation of energy I
ex-206-11.question: A spaceship of mass 120 000 kg flies forwards in outer space. Its rocket is fired to speed up the spaceship from 500 m s−1 to 600 m s−1 in 20 s. Assume that the power provided by the rocket is constant and the resistive force acting on the spaceship is negligible. Find the power of the rocket.
ex-206-11.answer:
KE 1 + work done by rocket = KE2

12mu2+Pt=12mv2

P=12m(v2−u2)t

P=12×120 000×(6002−5002)20

=3.3×108 W

The power of the rocket is 3.3×108 W.

ex-206-12.title: Power and conservation of energy II
ex-206-12.question:
A boat of mass 2500 kg moves along a straight line at a constant

acceleration of 1 m s−2. At time t = 0, its velocity is 2 m s−1. The average

power output of its engine is 12 kW from t = 0 to t = 4 s. Assume the

resistive force acting on the boat is constant. By considering the energy conversion of the boat, find the magnitude of the resistive force acting on the boat.
ex-206-12.answer:
KE1 + work done by engine = KE2 + work done against resistive force f

12mu2 + Pt = 12mv2 + fs .................... (1)

Take forwards as positive.

u = +2 m s−1, a = +1 m s−2, t = 4 s, v = ?, s = ?

v = u + at = 2 + 1 × 4

= 6 m s−1

s = ut + 12at2 = 2 × 4 + 12 × 1 × 42

= 16 m

Substitute into (1):

12 × 2500 × 22 + 12 000 × 4 = 12 × 2500 × 62 + f × 16

f = 500 N

The magnitude of the resistive force is 500 N.
ex-206-12.think:
1 Why is the instantaneous power output of the boat engine at t = 4 s larger than 12 kW?

2 Find the instantaneous power output of the boat engine at t = 4 s.
ex-206-12.thinkAnswer:
1 The driving force is constant because both the acceleration and resistance are constant. The instantaneous power P=Fv increases as the boat speeds up. Its final speed, 6 m s-1, exceeds the average speed, 4 m s-1, so its final power exceeds the average power of 12 kW.

2 F=ma+f=2500×1+500=3000 N. At t=4 s, v=u+at=2+1×4=6 m s−1. Thus P=Fv=3000×6=18 000 W=18 kW.
